content: Disjunctive cognition is a phenomenon commonly observed in dreams, first identified by psychoanalyst Mark Blechner. It occurs when two aspects of cognition do not align with each other. The dreamer is aware of this mismatch, yet it persists without resolution. The most frequent example of this disjunction is between appearance and identity. For instance, a dreamer might think, I knew it was my mother, even though it didn’t look like her. In such cases, the dreamer recognizes the identity of a character, even though their appearance does not correspond to that identity. Despite this incongruity, these dreams are not typically experienced as bizarre. In waking life, however, such a statement would be considered psychotic. In waking reality, most people would assume they had misidentified the person and would correct themselves, but this does not happen in dreams. Disjunctive cognition can also involve the perception of time. It is common to dream of being an adult while revisiting a time and place from one’s childhood. In such dreams, the perceived age of the dreamer is disjunctive with the setting of the dream. Conversely, it is less common to dream of oneself as a child in a setting from one’s adulthood. However, it is frequent to dream of other people, particularly those known at an earlier age, appearing in the present. This is especially common in the dreams of individuals who have lost close relatives. For example, Aharon Appelfeld described a dream in which he saw his parents, who had not aged since they were last together 63 years ago in Prague. Their faces expressed amazement at his aging, and they were briefly united in mutual astonishment. He felt he had something important to tell them, but, as is often the case in profound dreams, he was unable to articulate it. Blechner refers to disjunctive cognitions as the commonplace bizarreness of dream life. While some events in dreams feel bizarre to the dreamer, disjunctive cognitions typically do not. Another example of dream bizarreness is the interobject, where the dreamer perceives something that is a blend of two objects. For instance, one might dream of something between a swimming pool and an aqueduct or between a cell phone and a baby. Disjunctive cognitions provide insights into how the brain is organized. Blechner has proposed that when disjunctive cognitions occur, the two aspects of cognition that are disjointed are processed in different parts of the brain, and their integration is either suppressed or altered during sleep. Disjunctive cognitions involving the mismatch between a person’s appearance and their identity suggest the existence of two distinct brain systems responsible for these aspects of perception. This hypothesis is supported by research in neuropsychology and neurobiology. For example, individuals who have suffered strokes or other brain injuries may develop a condition known as prosopagnosia. A person with prosopagnosia might look at their spouse of 50 years, see all their features clearly, yet fail to recognize who they are. In such cases, the visual processing of the face remains intact, but the ability to recognize the face is impaired. Another related phenomenon is Capgras syndrome, in which a person believes that a close relative is actually an impostor. Here, the features of the relative are recognizable, but their identity is not perceived as genuine. Similarly, in Fregoli syndrome, a person may mistakenly identify strangers as people they know. In all these syndromes, there is a disjunction between the appearance of a person and their perceived identity. Neurobiological research has identified distinct areas of the brain responsible for facial recognition. In humans, recognizing unfamiliar faces activates one region of the brain (the fusiform region), while recognizing familiar faces also involves another area (the lateral midtemporal cortex). A similar division of function has been observed in macaque monkeys. These findings suggest that the process of recognizing faces is managed by specialized brain regions that are separate from those involved in analyzing the general features of objects. Since the brain has separate systems for determining what a person looks like and who the person is, this division of labor may underlie not only disjunctive cognitions but also the phenomenon of transference. In psychoanalytic treatment, patients often experience transference, in which the psychoanalyst is perceived as being very similar to someone from the patient’s past. As with disjunctive cognitions in dreams, the patient might feel, You look like Dr. X, but you feel like my mother. The distinct brain areas involved in recognizing what a person looks like and who the person is may provide a neurobiological basis for transference.
